questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Independent horizontal and vertical motion of a projectile
questions.learningObjective: identify which velocity component of a projectile changes during flight
questions.stem: A ball leaves a level surface with a velocity of 12.0 m/s at 30.0 degrees above the horizontal, and air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the two components of its velocity during the flight is correct?

options.text: The horizontal component stays 10.4 m/s while the vertical component changes steadily
Both components change, because the launch angle fixes the direction of the acceleration
options.misconception: believes the acceleration points along the launch direction rather than straight down

options.text: The total speed stays 12.0 m/s, because no force acts on a body in flight
options.misconception: believes a force-free path must have constant speed

options.text: The horizontal component shrinks as the ball rises, because gravity pulls backwards
options.misconception: believes gravity has a horizontal component opposing the motion

questions.explanation: Gravity is the only force once the ball is airborne, so the acceleration is 9.80 m/s^2 straight down with no horizontal part at all, and the horizontal velocity can therefore never change. Its value is fixed at the launch speed times the cosine of 30.0 degrees, which is 10.4 m/s, and it stays 10.4 m/s for the whole flight. The vertical component is the launch speed times the sine of 30.0 degrees, which is 6.00 m/s, and that component is what the downward acceleration works on, decreasing by 9.80 m/s every second. The total speed therefore does change even though no horizontal force exists, because the two components combine differently at different moments, and it is smallest at the top of the path.
questions.hint: The acceleration of a projectile is always vertically downward, whatever the launch direction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Where a projectile reaches its maximum height
questions.learningObjective: state the condition that defines the top of a projectile path
questions.stem: A stone is thrown steeply upward and slows as it rises. What is true at the instant it reaches the top of its path?

options.text: The upward velocity has fallen to zero while the acceleration stays downward
The total speed is zero there, and it is zero at no other point of the path
options.misconception: believes a zero vertical velocity means a zero total speed

options.text: The acceleration becomes zero there, because the air has stopped pushing
options.misconception: believes the air resistance switches the acceleration off at the top

options.text: The upward and downward air forces happen to be equal in size there
options.misconception: believes force balance is what marks the top of the path

questions.explanation: Only the vertical component changes during flight, and it decreases at a steady 9.80 m/s each second. The top of the path is exactly the moment that component reaches zero, so the rise stops and the fall begins. The acceleration is unchanged at that instant, because the cause of the acceleration, gravity, is still pulling the same way; zero velocity is a condition on the velocity, not on the force. The total speed is not zero there, since the horizontal component is untouched by gravity, so a projectile launched at an angle still moves sideways at the top. Treating a zero component as a zero speed is the common slip, and it is the same slip as saying a car has stopped because its forward velocity momentarily vanished.
questions.hint: Ask which component of the velocity is being reduced by the acceleration.

questions.topic: Launch angle that maximises range over level ground
questions.learningObjective: identify the launch angle that gives the largest range at a fixed speed
questions.stem: A ball is launched at a fixed speed over flat ground, landing at the same height from which it was launched. Which launch angle gives the greatest horizontal range?

options.text: 45 degrees, because the range contains the sine of twice the angle
60 degrees, because a steeper flight keeps the ball aloft for longer
options.misconception: believes a longer flight time outweighs a smaller horizontal speed

options.text: 30 degrees, because most of the launch speed is then horizontal
options.misconception: believes maximising the horizontal speed alone maximises the range

options.text: 90 degrees, because a vertical launch gives the longest total path
options.misconception: believes total path length and horizontal range are the same quantity

questions.explanation: The range over level ground is the launch speed squared times the sine of twice the launch angle, divided by the acceleration of gravity. The speed and the gravity are fixed, so the whole question is what value of the sine of twice the angle can be obtained, and the largest possible value of a sine is 1. That happens when twice the angle is 90 degrees, so the angle itself is 45 degrees. The tempting argument that a steeper launch wins because it stays in the air longer is wrong because a steeper launch also throws away horizontal speed: at 60 degrees the flight lasts 22 percent longer than at 45 degrees but the horizontal speed is 29 percent smaller, and the product of the two is only 0.866 of the 45 degree range, so the two effects do not cancel in favour of the steeper launch.

questions.topic: Terminal velocity as force balance
questions.learningObjective: explain what balances at the terminal velocity of a falling body
questions.stem: A sphere dropped in a fluid settles to a steady speed and falls at that speed forever. What must be true of the forces on the sphere at that steady speed?

options.text: The upward drag equals the weight, so the net force and the acceleration vanish
The upward drag is half the weight, so the sphere still accelerates downward
options.misconception: believes a steady speed requires a small residual net force

options.text: The weight has vanished, because a moving object is not supported
options.misconception: believes weight disappears once the object is in free motion

options.text: The upward drag slightly exceeds the weight, so the speed grows without bound
options.misconception: believes an overshoot is what produces a constant speed

questions.explanation: A constant speed in a straight line means the acceleration is zero, and by the second law that requires the net force to be zero. The only two forces on a falling sphere are its weight downward and the drag upward, so the two must be equal in size at the terminal speed. That is also why the speed cannot grow without bound: as the speed rises, the drag rises, so once drag catches weight the net force vanishes and nothing further accelerates. A steady speed never requires a residual net force; the opposite is true, since a residual net force in the direction of motion would mean the speed was still changing.
questions.hint: Use the second law: a steady speed means a zero acceleration.

questions.topic: Ballistic coefficient and relative deceleration
questions.learningObjective: relate the ballistic coefficient to the rate of slowing in flight
questions.stem: Two projectiles have the same shape and the same drag coefficient, but one has twice the mass of the other at the same frontal area. Which statement about their ballistic coefficients and their flight is correct?

options.text: The heavier one has twice the ballistic coefficient and slows more slowly at a given speed
The heavier one has half the ballistic coefficient, because mass makes drag worse
options.misconception: believes more mass always means more deceleration in air

options.text: Both have the same ballistic coefficient, because shape alone fixes the drag
options.misconception: believes the drag coefficient by itself determines the deceleration

options.text: The heavier one has four times the ballistic coefficient, because mass enters twice
options.misconception: believes the cross-sectional area of a same-shape body scales with its mass

questions.explanation: The ballistic coefficient is the mass divided by the product of the drag coefficient and the frontal area. For the same shape the area is the same number, so doubling the mass doubles the ratio. The deceleration caused by drag works out to be the drag divided by the mass, and with the drag written as one half times the air density times the drag coefficient times the area times the speed squared, the mass cancels down to a single factor of the inverse ballistic coefficient. So at the same speed the heavier body decelerates more slowly, which is exactly why a golf ball flies further than a table tennis ball of comparable size.
questions.hint: The drag deceleration is proportional to the inverse of the ballistic coefficient.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: What conservation a two-body collision guarantees
questions.learningObjective: distinguish guaranteed conservation from conditional conservation in a collision
questions.stem: Two carts collide on a frictionless track and no other cart or hand touches them. Which quantity is certain to be unchanged by the collision, whatever happens to the individual speeds?

options.text: The total momentum of the two-cart system
The total kinetic energy, because the collision is over so quickly
options.misconception: believes a short collision time means no energy is lost

options.text: The kinetic energy of the heavier cart, which the lighter one cannot affect
options.misconception: believes energy can only be moved between bodies, never lost

options.text: The speed of each cart separately, because the track is frictionless
options.misconception: believes a frictionless track freezes each body's own speed

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation is a statement about the system, not about the parts. The two carts exert equal and opposite forces on each other through the contact, so the internal forces cancel in the total momentum balance, and with no external horizontal force acting the total cannot change. Kinetic energy has no such protection, because the same pair of internal forces does equal and opposite work only over the displacement of each body, and those displacements are generally different. The contact squeezes the carts, stores energy in the deformation, and hands back less than it received, so kinetic energy normally falls. That is why momentum is called a conservation law for any isolated collision while kinetic energy needs the extra condition of elastic behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement is about the system or about one part of it.

questions.topic: Perfectly inelastic collision as the largest energy loss
questions.learningObjective: state the energy consequence of a perfectly inelastic collision
questions.stem: A 2.00 kg cart rolling at 3.00 m/s latches onto a stationary 1.00 kg cart and the pair moves off together. Which statement about the energy accounting is correct?

options.text: Momentum is conserved and the kinetic energy loss is as large as the momentum allows
Kinetic energy is conserved, because the two carts end at one common speed
options.misconception: believes a common final speed implies an unchanged total energy

options.text: Momentum is not conserved, because the latch pulls the two carts together
options.misconception: believes an internal coupling can change the system momentum

options.text: Kinetic energy is conserved, because no external force acts along the track
options.misconception: believes the absence of external forces protects kinetic energy

questions.explanation: Once the carts are locked together there is only one final velocity left to determine, and momentum conservation fixes it at 2.00 m/s. That single outcome is also the one that loses the most kinetic energy, because the loss in any perfectly inelastic collision equals one half times the reduced mass times the square of the relative approach speed, and no other final arrangement can remove more. The initial kinetic energy here is 9.00 J and the final value is 4.00 J, so 5.00 J has gone into the deformation and heat. The claim that a common speed protects energy has the logic backwards: the common speed is precisely what forces the two bodies to give up their relative motion, and that relative motion is where the energy was.
questions.hint: Compare the initial and final kinetic energy once the common speed is known.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: What a coefficient of restitution of one guarantees
questions.learningObjective: interpret a coefficient of restitution of one
questions.stem: An experimenter reports a coefficient of restitution of exactly 1.00 for an impact between two blocks. Which statement is guaranteed by that measured value alone?

options.text: The relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach
The total kinetic energy is unchanged, even if an external force shoves one block during contact
options.misconception: reads a property of the relative speeds as a statement about energy in all circumstances

options.text: Both blocks leave the contact moving in opposite directions with equal speeds
options.misconception: believes elastic impacts always reverse both bodies

options.text: The contact force rose and fell in the same way for both blocks during the impact
options.misconception: believes one scalar impact parameter fixes the whole force history

questions.explanation: The coefficient of restitution is defined as the relative speed of separation divided by the relative speed of approach, so a value of one says precisely that the two relative speeds are equal, whatever forces were acting. Turning that into a statement about kinetic energy needs a second ingredient, namely that the total momentum of the pair is unchanged while the contact happens. When both hold, the two conditions force the kinetic energy to match, which is why an isolated impact with a coefficient of restitution of one is called elastic. Without isolation the same restitution value can still show an energy change, because an external agent can add or remove momentum while the bodies are in contact, so the energy claim is the conditional one, not the definitional one.
questions.hint: The coefficient of restitution is a ratio of two relative speeds.

questions.topic: Range of a launch at an angle over level ground
questions.learningObjective: compute the range of a projectile launched over level ground
questions.stem: A ball is launched at 20.0 m/s at 45.0 degrees above level ground, and it lands at the height from which it was launched. Take g as 9.80 m/s per second squared. What is the horizontal range in metres?
questions.explanation: The range formula for equal launch and landing heights is the launch speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, divided by the gravity, which here is 400 divided by 9.80 because the sine of 90 degrees is 1, giving 40.82 m. Working it out from the components instead, the horizontal speed is 20.0 times the cosine of 45.0 degrees, which is 14.14 m/s, and the time aloft is twice the vertical speed 14.14 m/s divided by 9.80, which is 2.886 s, so the range is 14.14 times 2.886, again 40.82 m. The two routes agree, and the second one is worth doing because it shows where the answer comes from: half the flight time is spent climbing and half is spent falling back to the same level.
questions.hint: The range is the launch speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, divided by g.

questions.stem: A spherical projectile of diameter 0.0500 m and mass 0.0200 kg is fired through air of density 1.21 kg per cubic metre with a drag coefficient of 0.47. Using the area of the circular cross-section, what is its ballistic coefficient in kilograms per square metre?

The check that the number is physically sensible is that the units come out as kilograms per square metre, and a larger value means less deceleration at a given speed. Dividing by the radius rather than its square is the usual slip here, and it would make the value four times too large.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why the rise and fall of a projectile take equal times
questions.learningObjective: explain the symmetry between the rising and falling parts of a flight
questions.stem: Explain why the rising and falling parts of a projectile's flight take equal times when it lands at its launch height, and state what changes when the landing point is lower than the launch point.

answer.exemplar: The vertical motion is governed by a constant downward acceleration, and that single fact settles the question. While the body rises its vertical velocity starts at some positive value and shrinks at a steady rate until it reaches zero; from that zero value, under exactly the same constant downward acceleration, the vertical velocity becomes increasingly negative, and the sequence of values on the way down is the mirror image of the sequence on the way up. A constant acceleration makes the position a quadratic function of time, and that parabola is symmetric about its vertex, so the body retraces the same heights in the same order, and the height of the launch point is reached again after twice the time taken to reach the top. Working a case with g equal to 9.80 metres per second squared and a vertical launch speed of 15.0 metres per second, the time to the top is 15.0 divided by 9.80, which is 1.531 s, and the time back down to the same level is again 1.531 s, giving 3.062 s in total. If the landing point is lower than the launch point, the fall continues past the launch height, so the descent takes longer than the ascent and the total time increases; the equality of the two halves survives only for a landing at the launch height, or more generally whenever the two heights are the same.

questions.explanation: A stem that asks why two halves of a flight match is really asking about the shape of the height against time curve, and a constant downward acceleration is what gives that curve its symmetry. The explanation has to say which quantity is constant, because that is the assumption the symmetry rests on, and it has to connect the vanishing vertical velocity at the top to the repeat of every height on the way down. A numerical check with a 15.0 m/s vertical launch and g of 9.80 makes the claim concrete, and the closing sentence has to name the condition under which the symmetry fails, which is a landing height different from the launch height.
questions.hint: A constant acceleration makes the height a symmetric quadratic in time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why momentum settles a perfectly inelastic collision
questions.learningObjective: explain why momentum rather than energy fixes a sticking collision
questions.stem: Explain why the final speed of two bodies that stick together is fixed by momentum conservation rather than by energy conservation, and say where the kinetic energy goes.

answer.exemplar: Once the two bodies are locked together there is only one unknown left in the problem, the shared speed, and one equation is needed to pin it down. Momentum conservation is the equation that applies: the internal contact forces between the two bodies are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so they cannot change the total momentum of the pair, and with no external force along the line of motion the total momentum is the same before and after. A 0.200 kilogram trolley at 10.0 metres per second joining a stationary 0.300 kilogram trolley therefore leaves the pair at 0.200 times 10.0 divided by 0.500, which is 4.00 metres per second. Energy conservation cannot be used in its place, and the reason is structural: the contact between the bodies is not ideal, so the kinetic energy of relative motion is converted into deformation, heat and sound within the bodies. The initial kinetic energy is one half times 0.200 times 100, which is 10.0 joules, and afterwards it is one half times 0.500 times 16.0, which is 4.00 joules, so 6.00 joules has left the mechanical account. The loss has a definite size, equal to one half of the reduced mass times the square of the relative approach speed, which is one half times 0.120 times 100, again 6.00 joules, and no other final arrangement of the same total momentum could have lost more.

questions.explanation: A good answer has to count what is left to determine once the bodies are locked together, because that is the argument for needing only one equation, and it has to name momentum conservation as the unconditional law for an isolated pair. The exemplar then shows the arithmetic for the sticking case and identifies the size of the loss, so the reader can see that the energy is not missing but converted. Without the reduced-mass statement the loss looks like an arbitrary subtraction, and the whole point of the item is that it is not.
questions.hint: Count the unknowns after the bodies stick, and ask which conservation law is unconditional.

The two axes therefore produce different sets of terms yet agree on the answer, and the friction at the foot is 42.4 newtons against a normal force of 147 newtons, so the smallest usable coefficient of friction is 0.289. Quoting a torque without naming the axis is therefore not a complete statement, and the value half the tangent of the angle is the one tied to this geometry.

The friction coefficient that comes out of it is the payoff, so the answer has to end with the number and the condition it applies under.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: A collision claim that momentum accounting contradicts
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about a collision outcome against momentum conservation
questions.stem: A report claims that when a 1.00 kg cart at 4.00 m/s strikes a stationary 1.00 kg cart head-on on a frictionless track, both carts afterwards move forward together at 4.00 m/s. Explain why momentum accounting rules this out and what the outcome must actually be.

answer.exemplar: The claim fails on the simplest possible bookkeeping. The incoming momentum of the pair is 1.00 times 4.00, which is 4.00 newton seconds, and the claimed outcome carries a momentum of 2.00 times 4.00, which is 8.00 newton seconds, so the claimed final state has twice the momentum of the initial state. No internal contact force can produce that, because the two carts exert equal and opposite forces on each other and their contributions to the total momentum cancel exactly. Something outside the pair would have to be involved, and the report specifies a frictionless track with nothing else touching the carts, so the outcome is impossible. The only outcome consistent with the initial momentum of 4.00 newton seconds is one in which the two final velocities add, weighted by mass, to 4.00 metres per second for the pair. If the collision is elastic the familiar result is that the striking cart stops and the other leaves at 4.00 metres per second, which carries momentum 0 plus 4.00, exactly the incoming value. If the carts instead lock together, as the report assumes, momentum conservation forces the shared speed to be 2.00 metres per second, not 4.00, and the kinetic energy then falls from 8.00 joules to 4.00 joules. Halving the speed is the unavoidable price of making two bodies share one velocity, and forgetting that factor is what the claim gets wrong.

questions.explanation: The claim is refuted by the simplest possible check, which is that the stated outcome carries twice the momentum of the stated initial state, so the exemplar opens with that arithmetic rather than with theory. It then has to show what the consistent outcome actually is, in both the elastic and the sticking case, because an evaluation that only says the claim is wrong leaves the reader without the correction. The last sentence names the specific error in the claim, which is forgetting that two bodies sharing one velocity must share it at half the original speed when their masses are equal.
questions.hint: Compare the total momentum of the pair before the collision with the total momentum claimed after it.

questions.learningObjective: identify an impossible entry in a table of centripetal force data
questions.stem: Four bodies move in circles and a technician logs the mass, the speed, the radius and the inward force each one needs. Which of the four logged rows cannot be correct?

options.text: 1.00 kg at 3.00 m per second on 2.00 m needing 4.50 N
options.misconception: believes the force follows from mass and speed alone, with no radius

options.text: 2.00 kg at 4.00 m per second on 3.00 m needing 10.7 N
options.misconception: believes a bigger mass at the same speed always needs twice the force

options.text: 3.00 kg at 5.00 m per second on 1.50 m needing 50.0 N
options.misconception: believes a larger radius calls for a larger inward force at a fixed speed

options.text: 0.500 kg at 6.00 m per second on 2.00 m needing 4.50 N

questions.explanation: Each row has to satisfy the relation that the inward force is the mass times the square of the speed divided by the radius, and working that out row by row gives 4.50, 10.67, 50.0 and 9.00 newtons. The first three rows match those values, the second to the precision of the table, while the fourth lists 4.50 newtons where 9.00 is required. The 0.500 kilogram body is moving at 6.00 metres per second, so the square of the speed is 36.0, multiplied by the mass gives 18.0, and dividing by the 2.00 metre radius gives 9.00 newtons, so the logged value is half of what is needed and the body would swing outward along its path rather than staying on the circle.
questions.hint: Compute the mass times the speed squared divided by the radius for every row and compare.
